title: Folic acid before and in early pregnancy
text: Folic acid tablets taken from before pregnancy into the first weeks lower the chance of spine and brain defects such as spina bifida. Food alone usually isn't enough, so ask your doctor about a tablet.

title: Check iron before taking iron tablets
text: Thalassemia trait can cause low hemoglobin even when iron is normal. Taking iron for a long time without a proven deficiency doesn't help and can build up in the body. Ask for a ferritin test first.

title: Don't go gluten-free before the test
text: Keep eating wheat until the celiac blood test is done. If celiac disease is confirmed, the treatment is a lifelong, strict gluten-free diet planned with a dietitian. Rice, millets (jowar, bajra, ragi), dal and besan are naturally gluten-free.

title: Milk trouble doesn't mean no dairy
text: Many people who digest lactose poorly can still have curd and small amounts of milk with meals. If you cut down on milk, get calcium from foods like ragi, sesame (til) and green leafy vegetables.

title: Avoid fava beans until G6PD is checked
text: Fava (broad) beans can break down red blood cells in people with G6PD deficiency. Until you are tested, avoid them, and tell any doctor or pharmacist before starting a new medicine.

title: Food helps cholesterol, but may not be enough
text: Eating less saturated fat (ghee, butter, vanaspati, fried snacks) and more fibre (oats, dal, vegetables, whole grains) helps lower LDL. In familial hypercholesterolaemia, diet alone is usually not enough and medicines are needed, so don't use diet as a reason to delay seeing a doctor.

title: Skip the DNA diet test
text: Personal diet advice works as well when it is based on what you eat and your blood tests as when it is based on your genes. A dietitian and a routine blood test are a better use of money.

title: PKU: the diet is the treatment
text: PKU is treated with a lifelong low-phenylalanine diet and a special medical formula, managed by a metabolic team. Women with PKU need strict control before and during pregnancy to protect the baby.

title: Galactosemia: no milk sugar
text: Classic galactosemia is managed by avoiding milk and other foods containing lactose and galactose, with a metabolic dietitian. Calcium and vitamin D then need attention.

title: Celiac disease: strict gluten-free, for life
text: Avoid wheat, barley and rye completely, including hidden sources such as some spice mixes and packaged foods. A dietitian helps you plan meals around rice, millets, dal and besan.

title: Familial hypercholesterolaemia: diet plus medicine
text: A low saturated-fat, high-fibre diet is part of treatment, but FH almost always needs cholesterol-lowering medicines too. Close relatives should get their cholesterol checked.

title: G6PD deficiency: avoid fava beans
text: Avoid fava (broad) beans and check with a doctor or pharmacist before any new medicine. Most other foods are fine.

title: Thalassemia major: no extra iron
text: Regular transfusions already load the body with iron. Don't take iron tablets or iron tonics unless your thalassemia doctor says so, and follow your chelation plan.

title: Eat a balanced Indian thali
text: None of these food tips replace a doctor or dietitian. For everyday eating, ICMR-NIN's guidelines suggest a varied plate: cereals and millets, dal or other protein, plenty of vegetables and fruit, some milk or curd, and less sugar, salt and fried food.
